newsitem.title: GERMANY: G7 expected to try to stabilise dollar in Berlin.
newsitem.headline: G7 expected to try to stabilise dollar in Berlin.

text.p: The world's financial leaders are expected to try to sell a message of foreign exchange stability in one-day talks on Saturday amid concern from some that a sharp rally in the dollar may be going too far, too fast.

While the rise in the dollar has brought welcome relief to European countries struggling to cut budget deficits and bring down record unemployment, its climb against the yen has left the Japanese currency on the edge of weakness.

"Some G7 countries have expressed concern about the recent declines in their currencies," U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on the eve of talks between finance ministers and central bankers in the Group of Seven rich nations.

"Some will say the dollar has overshot the desirable level a little, notably vis-a-vis the yen," International Monetary Fund head Michel Camdessus said in an interview with French daily Le Monde on Friday. But he said the dollar, yen and European currencies were in a "zone of plausibility".
Official comments ahead of the talks in Berlin suggest ministers are likely to try to steady the dollar around current levels.
"Japan will ask G7 countries to stabilise the foreign exchange market," Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told reporters as he arrived in Berlin on Friday night.

But the G7 -- the United States, Canada, Japan, Britain, Germany, France and Italy -- have to find a form of words to hint that the dollar's rise has gone far enough without sending it into a tailspin on financial markets.
Only two years ago the G7 acted to bring the dollar back from record lows by calling for its orderly reversal.
Its rise has been particularly good for Europe, boosting exports and lifting growth as countries rush to cut budget deficits in time for the launch of a single currency in 1999.

It has also helped the United States, keeping import prices low and helping to maintain low inflation in its own economy, though U.S. carmakers are beginning to squeal about the effect of the dollar's rise on their exports.
But yen weakness, long a boost to Japanese exports, is now beginning to look risky for its financial system.
In a subtle change of tone for the United States, which has repeatedly said it favours a strong dollar, Rubin noted on Friday the currency had been strong "for some time now".
His comments sparked a dollar sell-off, highlighting market sensitivity to any hint the dollar's rise may be overdone.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Friday also indicated that stabilisation might be the order of the day.
"I remain of the opinion that a normalisation has taken place," he said. "At the same time, compared with levels we saw in 1993 and 1994, this is scarcely a change."
"What we must avoid above all are endless fluctuations which destabilise markets and penalise growth," French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told Reuters earlier this week.
The four European countries at the talks are also expected to brief their G7 partners on progress towards monetary union.
But putting on a united front will be hard, given Britain's reluctance to join the new euro from the start, and with a simmering row between Italy and Germany in the background.

Italy, Spain and Portugal have insisted they want to join the euro at the start while Germany is believed to fear that allowing in Europe's southern members too soon could weaken the single currency at its launch.
